title: The House that Jack Built - an interpretation.

commenti.body: I will have to disagree. I don't think the movie has much of Lynch (if any), I see more of Haneke or Gaspar Noe. when you say, "he feels no guilt; instead, he's confronted with his failure as an 'artist'. That's pure Haneke, it reminds me of the seven continent or Gaspar Noe's short film "Carne" almost like Tarantino, the violence is nothing else. we as a society want to give it a meaning and the serial killers being too full of themselves want to give their atrocities a meaning or in this case a correlation with 'art'. Then you have psychoanalysts that will say this and that to explain some cases and I think Von trier being who he is he's just telling us "There's nothing to it, he is just a fucking lunatic and that's all" I think that is why Jack suffers from that OCD and his cleaning the apartment like 20 times. he goes in circles wanting to erase what he did because it has no purpose no meaning. nothing. all the rest that you said it's a great analysis! I'm glad you like that movie. I love it too!

You made me like the end of this movie a lot more with this interpretation, even if it's very "Occurrence at Owl Creek."

I liked the movie pretty much all the way through until it felt like LVT had been beating me over the head with the whole "Virge" thing for some big surprise ending that was so obvious. 

I thought a better ending would've been for Jack to hear Virgil, disappear as he does in the "house," and that's it. We piece the rest together without any visuals but recall the conversations.

I thought it was rather tiresome to be dragged all the way though *The Divine Comedy* after like it was some big revelation.

I probably still would've preferred the movie ended without the supernatural visuals, but I do like it more thinking of it the way you've outlined.

I don't think the parts in hell are made up. I think the parts in the real world are. Jack is a hugely unreliable narrator pretending to be highly intelligent while downplaying his victims. A guilt and ego thing. 

First time I watched it I hated just how stupid Uma Thermans character seemed to be, until my friend pointed the above out. Jack is trying to impress Virgill but that spirals out of control when Virgil clearly doesn't care about his monologues or art. The last set up is Jack's actual competency. He'd just got lucky until now.

I at least partially agree. I don't think the stories he's telling are honest—or at least—the details are changed or exaggerated, for the reasons you say. Virgil even talks about it at one point; that the women in all his stories are unbelievably dumb. People are basically encouraging him to commit crimes throughout the film, he's practically begging to get caught.
Can't help but agree there. I think if you know Von Trier's miserable films you know this is a comedy.
Yeah if he wanted you to feel sad at the end the movie, you would know it.

The movie seems to be structured as a surreal filmmakers autobiography similar to 8,5 by Fellini (but a pastiche version of it, with added satirical essay of being an artist, and sort of a confession). Trier leaves many traces: Jack wears Lars leather jacket from his study times at film school, the list of various disorders are his own, the bus, women, and many others, the same. Many things are easier to decipher after watching Eric Nietzsche, 8,5, some of his written bios (Lasagna, Bjorgman) and his previous movies. I think, in some ways this movie has a spiritual link to American Psycho as in 2010 Ellis explains that "Patrick Bateman was about me"

Cool. It looks it's finally time for me to check out fellini. I do really like the meta art element. Its such a humble way for von trier to think about his career. 


When he's talking about violence in movies, it shows a bunch of older films, and then a clip of melancholia. I was suprised to see a von trier film in that montage but it makes sense now
